title: Why Some Bibles Skip From Acts 8:36 to Acts 8:38

spans.text: [And Philip said, 'If thou dost believe out of all the heart, it is lawful;' and he answering said, 'I believe Jesus Christ to be the Son of God;']
Εἶπε δὲ ὁ Φίλιππος, Εἰ πιστεύεις ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας, ἔξεστιν. Ἀποκριθεὶς δὲ εἶπε, Πιστεύω τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ εἶναι τὸν Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν.

significance.sourceObservation:
Read Acts 8 in the Berean Standard Bible and you go straight from verse 36 to verse 38. Verse 37 is not there. The same is true in the Berean Literal Bible, the Majority Standard Bible, Nestle's 1904 Greek edition, and the Robinson–Pierpont Byzantine Greek text of 2018 [S1, S2, S3, S5, S6]. Two of the seven editions compared here do print the sentence: the Greek Textus Receptus compilation of Robert Adam Boyd (2022), and Young's Literal Translation of 1898, which sets it inside square brackets [S4, S7]. "Textus Receptus" names the family of printed Greek New Testaments that began with Erasmus in 1516 and stood behind the King James Version [C7].

The difference lies in the Greek, not in English style: Boyd's edition and Robinson–Pierpont disagree about whether the sentence is there at all [S6, S7]. Nothing is hidden, though. BSB and MSB each attach a footnote at verse 36 reporting the Textus Receptus reading and printing it out [S1, S3]. In BSB and MSB, the main text skips verse number 37, while a publisher note at verse 36 prints the TR reading.
significance.interpretation:
The effect on the story is real but contained. With or without verse 37, Acts 8 says that Philip preached Jesus to the man reading Isaiah 53, that the man saw water and asked what was stopping him from being baptized, that Philip baptized him, and that he went away rejoicing (vv. 35–39) [S1]. Where the exchange is printed, the narrative pauses for a stated condition and a stated confession. Where it is not, the request and the rejoicing carry that weight without a quoted creed.

The verse is often recruited into arguments about who may be baptized. It cannot settle them, in either direction. The man in the chariot is an adult hearing the gospel from Philip; the passage says nothing about anyone else, and a sentence whose printing is disputed is a poor foundation for a doctrine. Lutherans locate the power of baptism in God's word and command rather than in the recipient's confession — the teaching of Augsburg Confession IX and the fourth part of Luther's Large Catechism, resting on other texts entirely [C6]. Whether verse 37 appears in your Bible does not move it.
